planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; astilbe wilts quickly in dry soil and needs reliable moisture through the growing season.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; astilbe wilts quickly in dry soil and needs reliable moisture through the growing season. Feathery, plume-like flower spikes in rich lavender-purple rise above deeply cut, fern-textured, bronze-tinged green foliage in early to midsummer, one of the older Arends hybrid astilbe cultivars still valued for its unusual purple flower color among the more common pinks, reds, and whites of the genus. Its plush, plume-like flower texture and reliable performance in consistently moist shade make it a classic choice for a woodland border, pond margin, or rain garden alongside hostas and ferns. Keep soil consistently moist through summer, top-dress with compost each spring, and divide congested clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry soil or hot afternoon sun and needs reliable moisture and shade to look its best.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; ligularia wilts dramatically in dry soil or hot afternoon sun and needs reliable moisture and shade to look its best. Large, rounded, deeply glossy purple-black leaves provide bold, dramatic foliage color from spring through fall, topped in mid- to late summer by bright orange-yellow, daisy-like flower clusters that create a striking contrast against the near-black leaves. One of the most popular dark-leaved ligularia cultivars for its combination of season-long foliage color and reliable summer bloom, it makes a bold accent for a shaded, consistently moist border or pond-edge planting where its water needs can be easily met. Keep soil constantly moist, since ligularia wilts visibly within hours of drying out even in shade, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade; Nana umbrella plant is a compact selection well suited to smaller water gardens where the full-sized species would be too large.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet soil at a pond or stream margin in partial shade; Nana umbrella plant is a compact selection well suited to smaller water gardens where the full-sized species would be too large. Large, rounded, umbrella-like leaves emerge on tall stalks after clusters of small pink flowers appear on separate, leafless stems in early spring, a compact dwarf selection of the native Pacific Northwest umbrella plant that keeps the species' bold, architectural foliage texture on a much smaller scale suited to a modest pond margin or bog garden. Its reduced size compared to the full species, which can reach several feet across, makes it a more practical choice for smaller water features where the straight species would quickly overwhelm the space. Keep soil consistently moist to wet, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring to control spread and maintain vigor.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Crested leopard plant tolerates more heat and humidity than many broad-leaved shade perennials, performing well in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Crested leopard plant tolerates more heat and humidity than many broad-leaved shade perennials, performing well in the Gulf South. Large, rounded, glossy leaves are crimped and ruffled along the margins into a distinctive crested, wavy edge unlike the smoother or spotted leaf forms of other leopard plant cultivars, giving this selection a bold, sculptural texture that stands out in a shaded bed even without its bright yellow daisy-like fall flowers. Native to coastal Japan and adapted to humid, salt-exposed conditions, it tolerates the heat and humidity of a Gulf South shade garden notably better than many other large-leaved shade perennials, making it a reliable textural anchor for a subtropical shade border. Keep soil consistently moist, protect from hard freezes in the colder part of its range, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring.
